components.note: 口 (mouth) — an exclamation made with the mouth
我 (wǒ) is a sound hint; ò is only a loose match

example.fact: 哦 is read with different tones for different attitudes: ò (falling) means 'oh, I see', ó (rising) means 'oh?' with surprise or doubt, and ǒ shows puzzlement. The character stays the same; the tone carries the mood.

components.note: 亻 (person) — the meaning link to 'but' has faded
旦 (dàn) gives the sound exactly

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dànshì méiyǒu shíjiān.
example.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.
example.fact: 但 on its own is fairly bookish; speech prefers 但是, 可是 or the softer 不过. It also appears in the pattern 不但…而且… 'not only…but also…'. Chinese does not pair it with 虽然 and an extra 'but' the way English sometimes does: 虽然…但是… uses both.

components.note: 衤 (cloth) — the original meaning of 被 is 'quilt, blanket'
皮 (pí) is the sound part, a weak match for bèi

example.pinyin: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le.
example.fact: 被 builds the passive: object + 被 + (doer) + verb. Traditionally it signals something unfortunate (被骗 'be cheated', 被偷 'be stolen'), though modern usage has widened it. The doer can be left out, as in the example. The 'quilt' sense survives in 被子.

components.note: 土 (earth) — the upper part; in older forms this was a figure swinging its arms, but today it reads as 'ground'
止 (foot) — a foot stepping along

example.fact: In modern Chinese 走 means 'walk' and 'leave' (我走了 'I'm off'), while 'run' is 跑. In classical Chinese it meant 'run', and that older sense survives in words like 奔走 and 走马 'galloping horse'.

components.note: 大 (big) — the main body of the character
丶 (dot) — a small mark added under 大 to show 'even bigger', i.e., excessive

example.fact: 太 + adjective + 了 can complain or praise: 太贵了 'too pricey', 太好了 'great!'. But 不太 is the mild 'not very': 不太好 'not so good'. Keep 大 (dà) and 太 (tài) apart: the extra dot is what separates them.

components.note: 田 (field) — the upper part; an old sense is a village or district, which fits fields
土 (earth) — the lower part, the land itself

example.english: The book is in the bag.
example.fact: 里 is the standard 'inside' word after nouns (家里, 包里) and is toneless there. In simplified writing 里 took over for the older 裡 'lining, inside', so one character now covers both 'inside' and the old unit of length (about 500 m).

components.note: 足 (foot) — the original meaning is the heel, then following
艮 (gèn) is a close sound match for gēn

example.english: I'm going together with a friend.
example.fact: 跟 is the casual, northern-style 'with/and', replacing 和 in speech: 我跟你说 'let me tell you'. 跟…一样 means 'the same as'. Its physical meaning 'heel' remains in 脚后跟 and 高跟鞋 'high-heeled shoes'.

components.note: The shape is built on a horizontal stroke over 冉; the modern form is best learned as a unit meaning 'again'

example.english: Please say it one more time.
example.fact: 再 is for repeats that haven't happened yet: 再来一杯 'another cup'. For repeats that already occurred, use 又: 他又来了. 再见 'goodbye' literally means 'see (you) again'.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the left part, linked to speech and sound
斤 (jīn) — a shorthand stand-in in this simplified form, not a literal axe-and-ear picture

example.fact: 听 means 'listen', while 听见 or 听到 means 'actually hear'. 听说 introduces hearsay: 听说他走了 'I hear he left'. The simplified 听 reuses an old character that meant 'to smile', borrowed to replace the more complex 聽.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — feelings; an older sense of 快 is 'pleased'
夬 (guài) gives the sound, a near match for kuài

example.pinyin: Nǐ zǒu de tài kuài le.
example.fact: 快 + verb means 'about to': 快到了 'almost there'. It also forms 快乐 'happy' and 快点儿 'hurry up'. As an adjective it describes speed: 快车 'express train'. Its first sense of 'pleased' explains why it appears in 快乐.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — asking about a person
隹 (zhuī) gives a rough sound hint

example.fact: 谁 is spoken shéi, with shuí as the older or more formal reading. The question word stays in the sentence slot of the answer: 谁来了？ 'Who came?' For 'everyone', 谁 + 都 works: 谁都知道 'everyone knows'.

components.note: 夕 (evening) — written twice; two evenings piled up suggest 'many'

example.english: There are a lot of people here.
example.fact: 多 before an adjective asks degree: 多大 'how old/big', 多远 'how far'. After a number it means 'and a bit more': 三十多个人. A noun usually needs 很 in front: 很多人, not 多人.

components.note: The shape's origin is debated; learn it as a unit meaning 'use'

example.pinyin: Wǒ kěyǐ yòng nǐ de shǒujī ma?
example.fact: 用 'use' appears in 用中文说 'say it in Chinese'. Negated it means 'no need to': 不用谢 'no need to thank me', 不用了 'no, thanks'. It also forms 有用 'useful' and 没用 'useless'.

components.note: A short mark below a long line, mirroring 上 'above'

example.fact: 下 means 'next' in 下个月 'next month' and 下次 'next time'. Chinese says 下雨 for 'rain' (literally 'rain falls') and 下班 for 'finish work'. It is also a verb: 下车 'get off the vehicle'.

components.note: 一 (one) — a stroke above, standing for the sky
大 (big/person) — the large figure beneath it; together they show 'what is above a person'

example.pinyin: Wǒ měi tiān dōu xué Zhōngwén.
example.fact: 天 covers both 'sky' and 'day': 天空 sky, 三天 three days, 天气 weather. Doubled as 天天 it means 'every day'. It also reaches into abstract uses: 老天 'heaven', 天才 'genius'.

components.note: 亻 (person) — an image or likeness of a person
象 (xiàng) gives the sound exactly; it is also the older word for 'image'

example.pinyin: Nǐ zhǎng de hěn xiàng nǐ bàba.
example.english: You look a lot like your dad.
example.fact: 像 is 'to resemble', and 像…一样 'just like…' makes similes. 好像 means 'it seems'. 像 was formed by adding 亻 to 象, which originally also meant 'image', long before it meant 'elephant' in everyday use.

components.note: An old form shows a snake, later borrowed for 'it'; 蛇 'snake' was created afterward by adding 虫

example.pinyin: Tā shì yì zhī kě'ài de xiǎo gǒu.
example.english: It is a cute little dog.
example.fact: 它 refers to things and animals; people are 他 or 她. In Chinese the subject 'it' is often dropped (很好吃 'it's tasty'). Plural is 它们. In Taiwan 牠 was traditionally used for animals, though 它 is common today.

components.note: 人 (person) — written twice, one person following another

example.fact: 从 gives a starting point: 从这里到那里 'from here to there'. 从来 means 'ever' and 从来不 'never'. Its roots are the picture of one person following another, which is the older meaning 'to follow'.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — searching by hand
戈 (spear) — the right-hand part; the character is explained as a person with a weapon looking for something, a memory aid

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài zhǎo wǒ de shǒujī.
example.fact: 找 is 'search for'; 找到 is 'found it', so they are different results. 找 can also mean 'to give change' (找您五块 'here's five yuan back') and 'to visit': 我来找你.

components.note: 日 (sun) — here the top part, a simplified shape of an old 'hat' form
取 (qǔ, to take) — the lower part; 最 once meant 'to excel by taking the top spot'

example.fact: 最 forms superlatives before an adjective or verb: 最大 'biggest', 最近 'recently', 最后 'last'. No 很 is needed. Don't confuse 最 (zuì) with 取 (qǔ); the top part differs.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — an approving word spoken aloud, as a memory aid
丁 (dīng) — the other part; the modern shape is best learned as a unit

example.fact: 可 mostly appears in compounds: 可以 'may', 可能 'maybe', 可爱 'cute', 可是 'but'. Alone in speech it adds emphasis: 你可来了 'you've finally come!' or 我可不去 'I'm certainly not going'.

components.note: Simplified from 為; the modern form is a shorthand and has no readable picture

example.fact: 为 is wèi when it means 'for': 为了 'in order to', 为什么 'why'. It is wéi when it means 'to be/act as': 成为 'become', 以为 'to (mistakenly) think'. The two readings are easy to mix up.

components.note: A person standing with arms stretched wide to show size

example.fact: 大 is 'big' and also the word for age: 你多大？ 'How old are you?' 大家 means 'everyone', and 大学 'university'. Be careful not to confuse 大 (dà) with 太 (tài), which has one extra dot.

components.note: 歹 (bone remains) — the left part, a radical for death and decay
匕 (spoon/person) — on the right; the pairing suggests a person beside remains, as a memory aid

example.fact: 死 is blunt, so polite speech says 去世 or 过世 for a person's death. As a degree word it means 'extremely': 累死了 'dead tired', 饿死了 'starving'. Because 四 (sì) sounds like 死 (sǐ), the number four is considered unlucky.

components.note: 冫 (two dots) — the left part
欠 (yawn, lack) — the right part; its link to 'occurrence' is not obvious today

example.pinyin: Wǒ qù guo liǎng cì Zhōngguó.
example.fact: 次 counts occurrences: 一次 'once', 第二次 'the second time'. Compare 遍 for a full run-through (读一遍 'read it through once'). It also means 'secondary': 次日 'the next day', 次要 'less important'.

components.note: 屮 (sprout) — a shoot rising
凵 (open container) — the sprout pushes out of it

example.fact: 出 works as a verb and as a direction ending: 走出来 'walk out', 看出 'make out'. In compounds: 出口 'exit', 出租车 'taxi', 出发 'set off', 出生 'be born'. The opposite is 入 or 进.

components.note: An old picture of a forked stick or shield, the root of many other senses

example.fact: 干 gàn is the colloquial 'do': 干活 'work', 干什么 'what for?'. The same simplified character is read gān 'dry' (干净 'clean') because 乾 'dry' and 幹 'to do' were both merged into 干 in simplification.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a spoken exclamation
黑 (hēi) gives the sound exactly

example.fact: 嘿 grabs attention informally, like 'hey'. Doubled as 嘿嘿 it is a sly chuckle. The similar 嗨 (hāi) is a borrowed 'hi' greeting. In writing, 嘿 is rarely used in formal text.

components.note: 亻 (person) — the suffix applies to people
门 (mén) gives the sound exactly

example.fact: 们 makes pronouns and some nouns plural: 我们, 你们, 他们, 朋友们. It does not go with a number: 三个朋友, not 三个朋友们. Animals and objects don't take it, except in fairy-tale style.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — spoken language
舌 (tongue) — the organ of speech; its sound link to huà is only loose

example.fact: 话 means 'words' or 'speech': 一句话 'a sentence', 电话 'telephone', 普通话 'Mandarin' ('common speech'). 说话 'to speak' is a verb-object phrase, so you can say 说了几句话.

components.note: An old picture usually explained as a beard; the connective sense is a later borrowing

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn piányi, érqiě hǎochī.
example.english: This restaurant is cheap, and tasty too.
example.fact: 而 is a formal connective for 'and' or 'but'. In speech it is mostly found in 而且 'moreover', 然而 'however', 因而 'therefore' and 而已 'that's all'. It is not used to join nouns the way 和 is.

meanings: suffix in 什么, 怎么, 这么

components.note: A simplified form of 麼; here it is a shorthand and has no readable picture

example.fact: 么 appears almost only in a few common words: 什么 'what', 怎么 'how', 这么 'so', 那么 'such', 多么 'how (much)'. Don't confuse 么 with 幺 (yāo), the 'one' read in phone numbers.

components.note: A sprout breaking out of the ground, matching the old sense of 'budding talent'

example.english: He doesn't get up until eight.
example.fact: 才 stresses that something is late or hard: 八点才起床 'only at eight'. Compare 就: 八点就起床 'already at eight'. The same sound gives 人才 'talented person' and 才能 'ability', which keep the older meaning.

components.note: Simplified from 兩; it suggests a pair of items under a frame

example.fact: 两 is 'two' before a measure word (两个人), while 二 is used for counting, ordinals and numbers: 二十, 第二. 两 also means a small number: 过两天 'in a couple of days'. It is the old unit 'tael' in weights too.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — an old sense of 错 is 'to inlay with metal'
昔 (xī) is a loose sound hint, not a close match

example.fact: 错 is 'wrong': 你错了, 没错 'right!'. It also forms 不错 'not bad', a common mild praise. Its original sense 'to inlay metal' survives in the old term 错金 'gold inlay'.

components.note: A drawing of a right hand with three fingers

example.fact: 又 is for repeats that have already happened (他又来了) and for 'both…and…': 又大又好 'both big and good'. For repeats still to come, use 再. 又 is a hand shape, which is why it appears in other hand-related characters.

components.note: A vertical stroke with two small marks, picturing tiny bits

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yì zhī xiǎo māo.
example.fact: 小 prefixes names for familiarity: 小王 'young Wang'. It also means 'humble' in 小店 'my humble shop'. The opposite is 大, and 小心 'be careful' literally means 'small heart'.

components.note: A line through the middle of a frame

example.fact: 中 is 'middle', as in 中国 'China' (the 'central country'). It is read zhòng when it means 'to hit': 中奖 'win a prize', 中毒 'be poisoned'. Be careful: 中 zhōng and 钟 zhōng sound alike.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — calling aloud
丩 (jiū) gives a close sound hint

example.fact: 叫 gives names: 我叫… 'I'm called…'. It means 'to call out' (叫他来 'tell him to come'), and in speech marks a passive: 我叫他骗了. 叫 plus a person is common for ordering a taxi: 叫出租车.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a vocal sound
恩 (ēn) gives the sound

example.fact: 嗯 is a backchannel sound whose tone sets the meaning: a falling tone agrees ('yes'), a rising tone asks 'what?', and a flat sound expresses thinking. Mainland dictionaries mark these as ń, ň, ǹ.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — a spoken duty or rule
亥 (hài) gives a close sound hint

example.fact: 该 means 'should' or 'it's time': 该吃饭了 'time to eat'. It can mean 'it's your turn' (该你了) and, strongly, 'must be' (这该是他的 'this must be his'). The full word 应该 is also very common.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — bamboo strips lined up evenly, the origin of 'equal'
寺 (sì) is a loose sound hint

example.fact: 等 is 'wait': 等我 'wait for me'. Doubled 等等 as a list ender means 'etc.', and 等 can mean 'class/grade' (一等奖 'first prize'). The word 平等 'equality' keeps the older sense of 'equal'.

components.note: 合 (hé, join) — the upper part, as in closing a grip
手 (hand) — the lower part, grasping

example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ ná wǒ de shū.
example.fact: 拿 is 'take in hand', unlike 带 (take along). It forms 拿手 'good at' and 拿出来 'take out'. In 把 sentences it often appears: 把书拿来 'bring the book'.

components.note: The shape's origin is debated; learn it as a unit

example.english: Today is even colder than yesterday.
example.fact: 更 (gèng) means 'even more' in comparisons: 更好 'even better'. It is read gēng when it means 'to change' (更新 'update') or an old watch of the night (三更半夜 'in the dead of night').

components.note: 邦 (bāng, country) — gives the sound exactly; it is also a hint of 'a group helping each other'
巾 (cloth) — the lower part, as in the older form 幫

example.english: Let me help you carry it.
example.fact: 帮 takes a person and a verb: 帮我开门 'help me open the door'. 帮忙 'to help out' is verb-object: 帮个忙 'do me a favour'. The formal word is 帮助. Simplified from 幫.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — an action done by hand
丁 (dīng) gives a close sound hint

example.fact: 打 is far more than 'hit': 打电话 'make a phone call', 打车 'take a taxi', 打伞 'hold an umbrella', 打折 'give a discount'. It is the verb of choice for many hand actions and ball sports.

components.note: 爫 (claw/hand) — the top part, a hand reaching
友 (friend) — the bottom part; the traditional 愛 had 心 'heart' in the middle, which simplification removed

example.fact: 爱 as 'love' is stronger than English in couples' talk: 我爱你 is used less casually than 'I love you'. As a habit verb it means 'fond of': 他爱吃辣 'He loves spicy food'. The simplified form drops the 心 of 愛, a fact Chinese learners often joke about.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — the lower part; a belt or band of cloth, the original sense of 带

example.english: I take my child to the park.
example.fact: 带 means 'carry along' or 'lead': 带路 'show the way', 带孩子 'look after a child'. It differs from 拿 'hold in hand'. As a noun it means 'belt' or 'zone': 一带 'the area'.

components.note: An old form shows a person under a bundle of grain; the harvest, which came once a year, came to mean 'year'

example.fact: 年 counts years: 三年, 去年 'last year', 明年 'next year'. 过年 means 'celebrate the Lunar New Year'. In its oldest sense it referred to the grain harvest. 年 is a measure of time only: use 岁 for age.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — spoken courtesy
青 (qīng) gives the sound, a close match for qǐng

example.fact: 请 + verb is the polite 'please': 请进 'please come in', 请问 'excuse me, may I ask'. 请客 means 'to treat someone', and 请假 'ask for leave'. It is also 'to hire': 请老师 'engage a teacher'.
